issues.legal_issue: A testamentary instrument must be proved through evidence establishing the testator’s execution and the attestation required by law.
material_facts: The propounder sought administration of an instrument said to be a will and produced two attesting witnesses and a registering officer.

One attesting witness could not recall whether the testator signed in his presence or whether he signed as an attesting witness, and said his signatures at registration were as an identifying witness.
The other attesting witness said he had not seen the testator sign, did not know the document’s contents, and had not been asked to attest it as a will.
The registering officer testified about the testator’s acknowledgment at registration but did not establish that the witnesses saw the testator sign or signed in the testator’s presence.
The evidence, considered together or separately, did not establish the required attestation or an intention to attest.
issues.conclusion: The instrument was not proved as a validly executed and attested will, so administration could not be granted on its basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, a will must be attested by at least two witnesses in the specified manner. Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, at least one available attesting witness must prove execution; the registration exception for other documents does not apply to wills. Proof of the testator’s signature alone is insufficient. The Court relied on Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam, which explains that the witness must prove the attestation required by Section 63(c), and on Bhaiya Guruji Dutt Singh v. Gangotri Dutt Singh concerning the need for an intention to attest.

predicates.testamentary_proceeding: A person seeks a grant of administration or other testamentary relief on the basis of an instrument said to be a will.
predicates.attesting_evidence_does_not_establish_re: The evidence of the available attesting witnesses does not establish that the testator signed or acknowledged the instrument and that the witnesses attested it in the required manner.
predicates.witness_signatures_lack_attesting_intent: The evidence shows that the witnesses signed only in another capacity or does not show that they intended their signatures to attest the will.

issues.definition: In a proceeding based on a will, if the evidence does not establish the required attestation or an intention to attest, the will is not proved.

issues.legal_issue: Other evidence may be used to prove a will when an attesting witness denies its execution or genuinely cannot recall it, but not merely when the witness’s evidence fails to prove execution and attestation.
material_facts: The propounder examined both attesting witnesses.
Neither witness denied that the instrument had been executed, nor did either fail to recollect the event of execution; their evidence was instead deficient in establishing execution and attestation.
The propounder sought to rely on the registering officer’s evidence as other evidence to establish the will.
issues.conclusion: The statutory route for proving execution through other evidence was unavailable, and the registering officer’s evidence could not cure the deficiencies in the attesting evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 71 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, permits other evidence if an attesting witness denies or does not recollect execution. It is a limited safeguard, not a substitute for Sections 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 and 68 of the Evidence Act, and cannot be used merely because the witness’s evidence is inadequate. The Court relied on Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam and distinguished M. B. Ramesh v. K. M. Veeraje Urs, where the witness’s evidence indicated a genuine failure to recollect a fact.

rule.if: testamentary_proceeding and attesting_witnesses_examined and testimony_fails_to_prove_execution and witnesses_neither_deny_nor_forget_execution

predicates.testamentary_proceeding: A person seeks a grant of administration or other testamentary relief on the basis of an instrument said to be a will.
predicates.attesting_witnesses_examined: One or more available attesting witnesses are called to give evidence about the instrument.
predicates.testimony_fails_to_prove_execution: The testimony of the attesting witnesses does not establish the execution and attestation required for the instrument.
predicates.witnesses_neither_deny_nor_forget_execut: The witnesses neither deny the execution of the instrument nor genuinely fail to remember that event.

issues.definition: In a proceeding based on a will, when attesting witnesses give inadequate evidence but neither deny nor genuinely forget execution, other evidence cannot be used to cure that inadequacy.

issues.legal_issue: An unnatural disposition that excludes close relatives with whom the testator had cordial relations may constitute a suspicious circumstance that the propounder must dispel.
material_facts: The alleged will left the property to a person outside the testator’s immediate family while the testator’s wife, children, and grandchildren were alive.
The evidence described the testator’s relationship with those family members as warm and cordial.
The Court considered the disposition unnatural, unfair, and improbable, and found that it cast doubt on the testator’s free and discerning state of mind.
issues.conclusion: The circumstances surrounding the disposition reinforced the doubt about the will’s validity and supported the refusal to grant administration on its basis.
issues.legal_principle: The propounder of a will must prove its essential execution requirements and remove legitimate suspicious circumstances; the evidence must be sufficient to satisfy the court’s conscience. An unnatural, improbable, or unfair disposition may be a suspicious circumstance. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B. N. Thimmajamma, Surendra Pal v. Dr. (Mrs.) Saraswati Arora, and Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur.

predicates.testamentary_proceeding: A person seeks a grant of administration or other testamentary relief on the basis of an instrument said to be a will.
predicates.disposition_unusually_excludes_close_fam: The alleged will gives property to someone outside the testator’s close family while excluding close relatives who would ordinarily be expected to benefit.
predicates.close_family_relationships_were_cordial: The evidence indicates that the testator had cordial relationships with the excluded close relatives.

issues.definition: In a proceeding based on a will, an unusually exclusionary disposition in the face of cordial family relationships is a suspicious circumstance requiring explanation.
